assessment: This study combines an impressive combination of experimental and computational approaches to probe the function of the cuticular pinnae, structures that form air-filled cavities around the tympanal ears on the forelegs of bush crickets. In many other species – including mammals – the external ears are known to play a critical role in helping to localize sounds. The results of this study show, however, that the very small resonant cavities formed by the pinnae in one particular bush cricket species are able to boost ultra-high frequency sound waves that lie well above the frequencies used for communicating with conspecifics. This raises the possibility that these structures may have evolved to assist bush crickets to detect the ultrasonic echolocation calls of their bat predators.
